---
title: "What do you do with a hole in the table?"
subtitle: "You will patch the holes by hand first, then teach it to a computer. All you need is arithmetic."
engine: knitr
---

Here are 24 people who filled in a short survey. Each dot is one person, placed by two numbers: how many years they have worked, and how much they earn in a year, in thousands. Six of them left the income box blank.

Real tables always have holes like these. Sensors fail, forms get skipped, signals drop. Nobody tells you this early on: every way of dealing with a hole changes the data. So you need to know what each one does before you choose.

## Which rows would you throw away?

The easiest thing to do with a row that has a hole is to throw the whole row away. Try it.

The figure cheats, so that you can check what happens. It shows the six blank incomes as squares, at the values those people would have written. In real life you would never see them. The forms that lost their income here lost it by pure chance: say, a cup of coffee went over a few pages.

Click each square to throw that row away. Watch the line: it is the average income of the rows you still have.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="holes-lab" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · 24 made-up people; six incomes went missing by chance"}
:::

The line wobbles a little and ends close to where it started. The dashed line is the true average, of all 24 incomes. Throwing six rows away left you with 18, and those 18 look like the 24 you started with.

Now suppose the blanks did not fall by chance. People who earn a lot are often the ones who skip the income question.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
This time the six blank incomes are mostly the highest ones. You throw those rows away. What does the average of the rows you keep do?

- **Stays about the same, like before.** That was true when the holes fell at random, because the rows you lost looked like the rows you kept. Here they do not.
- **Slides down.** Yes. The rows you throw away are the high earners, so what is left is mostly the lower ones.
- **Slides up.** That would happen if the lowest earners skipped the question. Here it is the highest.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="holes-lab" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · the same 24 people; this time the six highest earners left it blank"}
:::

The line slides down with every click and ends about 9 thousand below the truth. Nothing on the screen warns you. You just have a smaller table that gives the wrong answer.

So the first question about a hole is not "how do I fix it?" but "**why is it there?**" There are three kinds of answer:

- **By pure chance.** The coffee. Throwing those rows away is safe, as long as you still have enough rows left.
- **Because of something else you did record.** Say men skip a "weight" box more often than women, and you know who is a man. Throwing rows away is risky now.
- **Because of the missing value itself.** The high earners who skip the income box. Throwing rows away is dangerous, and you will not know unless you go looking.

### Now tell a computer

A computer cannot see the gaps in a picture. Each person is a pair of numbers, such as `(29, 92)`: 29 years at work and 92 thousand a year. A blank is written `None`, which is Python's word for "nothing here". The cell below fetches the 24 people from Fig. 1.

Press **Run**. The first time takes a few seconds while Python starts.

The code walks through the rows one at a time. `for i in range(len(points))` means "for every row number i, from 0 up to the number of rows". `if` checks something, and `else` says what to do when the check fails. `append` adds one thing to the end of a list. One blank is left: which number should go on the list of holes?

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import points, truth      # the 24 people; truth holds the real incomes, for checking only

complete = []                       # the rows that have both numbers
holes = []                          # the row numbers that have a blank
for i in range(len(points)):
    years, income = points[i]       # take the pair apart
    if income is None:              # a blank
        holes.append(____)
    else:
        complete.append((years, income))

print(len(points), "rows.", len(holes), "have a hole:", holes)
print("Row", holes[-1], "is", points[holes[-1]])

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "vlines": [points[i][0] for i in holes],     # a thin line where each hole is
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": [str(len(complete)) + " complete rows", str(len(holes)) + " holes"],
}
```
::: {.py-solution}

Python counts rows from 0, so the first row is row 0, and `holes[-1]` means the last one on the list. The thin upright lines in the picture are the holes: you know how long those people have worked, but not what they earn. `[points[i][0] for i in holes]` is a short way to make a list: the years of every row in `holes`. `str` turns a number into text, so it can be joined to words with `+` for the notes beside the picture.

## What would you write in the hole?

Throwing rows away loses everything else those people told you. The other choice is to write something in the hole. Take the last one: a person with 29 years at work.

Drag the star up or down to the income you would write in for them. Then press the buttons beside the picture to see two ideas you might have had.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="holes-lab" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 3 · fill one hole: your guess, the average of the rest, and what a line says"}
:::

The first idea is **the average of the rest**: 61.1, the typical income in the table. The second uses the other number you do have. People who have worked longer tend to earn more, so draw the line that runs closest to the complete rows, and read off where it is at 29 years.

::: {.ask}
In real life you never see the true income. How could you tell whether a way of filling is any good?

- **You can't. You just have to trust it.** You can do better. You have 18 incomes you do know.
- **Hide some values you do know, fill them, and compare.** Yes. That is what the figure's last button lets you do, because this made-up table has the answers. With real data you hide a few known values on purpose and see how close the fill comes.
:::

Press *show the real value*. The line comes much closer than the average, because it uses what you know about this person: they have worked a long time.

### Now tell a computer

Filling with the average first. `def` gives a set of steps a name, so you can use them again: from now on `average(values)` means "add them up and divide by how many". `[p[1] for p in complete]` makes a list of the second number of every pair, the incomes. One blank: what goes in the hole?

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def average(values):
    return sum(values) / len(values)          # add them up, divide by how many

incomes = [p[1] for p in complete]            # the 18 incomes you have
avg = average(incomes)

filled = []                                   # a new table, with the holes filled in
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        filled.append((years, ____))          # what goes in the hole?
    else:
        filled.append((years, income))        # keep what was written

print("Average of the incomes you have:", round(avg, 1))
print("Row", holes[-1], "is now", (filled[holes[-1]][0], round(filled[holes[-1]][1], 1)))

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "stars": [filled[i] for i in holes],      # the filled-in rows
    "hlines": [avg],
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": ["average " + str(round(avg, 1)), "6 holes filled"],
}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def average(values):
    return sum(values) / len(values)          # add them up, divide by how many

incomes = [p[1] for p in complete]            # the 18 incomes you have
avg = average(incomes)

filled = []                                   # a new table, with the holes filled in
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        filled.append((years, avg))           # the hole gets the average of the rest
    else:
        filled.append((years, income))        # keep what was written

print("Average of the incomes you have:", round(avg, 1))
print("Row", holes[-1], "is now", (filled[holes[-1]][0], round(filled[holes[-1]][1], 1)))

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "stars": [filled[i] for i in holes],      # the filled-in rows
    "hlines": [avg],
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": ["average " + str(round(avg, 1)), "6 holes filled"],
}
```
:::
:::

Compare the average it prints with the one in Fig. 3. All six stars sit in one flat row, whatever their years at work.

Now the line. You met the line that runs closest to the points when you fitted a line: of all the straight lines, it has the smallest total of squared misses. The cell below works it out from the complete rows, in full, so you can read every step. Find the middle of the years and the middle of the incomes. Then the slope, which is how much income goes up for each extra year, comes from one division, and the line is made to pass through both middles.

`for x, y in table` takes each pair in turn and calls its two numbers x and y. One blank, in the last function: where is the line at a given number of years?

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def fit(table):
    xs = [p[0] for p in table]                # the years
    ys = [p[1] for p in table]                # the incomes
    mx = average(xs)                          # the middle of the years
    my = average(ys)                          # the middle of the incomes
    top = 0
    bottom = 0
    for x, y in table:
        top = top + (x - mx) * (y - my)       # positive when a row is above both middles, or below both
        bottom = bottom + (x - mx) * (x - mx) # how spread out the years are
    slope = top / bottom                      # income gained for each extra year
    height = my - slope * mx                  # the line goes through both middles
    return height, slope

height, slope = fit(complete)

def on_line(years):
    return height + slope * ____              # where is the line at this many years?

line_filled = []
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        line_filled.append((years, on_line(years)))
    else:
        line_filled.append((years, income))

print("Height", round(height, 1), "and slope", round(slope, 2))
print("At 29 years the line says", round(on_line(29), 1))

from page import my_fill                      # where you left the star in Fig. 3
i = holes[-1]                                 # the row you filled by hand: 29 years
print("Row", i, "- you said", my_fill, " average", round(avg, 1), " line", round(on_line(29), 1), " real", truth[i])

frames = []
for step in range(7):
    t = step / 6                              # 0 at the start, 1 at the end
    stars = []
    for i in holes:
        y = avg + (line_filled[i][1] - avg) * t    # slide from the average to the line
        stars.append((points[i][0], y))
    frames.append({
        "points": complete, "stars": stars,
        "lines": [[(0, height), (32, on_line(32))]],
        "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
        "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
        "notes": ["slope " + str(round(slope, 2)), "height " + str(round(height, 1))],
    })
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def fit(table):
    xs = [p[0] for p in table]                # the years
    ys = [p[1] for p in table]                # the incomes
    mx = average(xs)                          # the middle of the years
    my = average(ys)                          # the middle of the incomes
    top = 0
    bottom = 0
    for x, y in table:
        top = top + (x - mx) * (y - my)       # positive when a row is above both middles, or below both
        bottom = bottom + (x - mx) * (x - mx) # how spread out the years are
    slope = top / bottom                      # income gained for each extra year
    height = my - slope * mx                  # the line goes through both middles
    return height, slope

height, slope = fit(complete)

def on_line(years):
    return height + slope * years             # start at the height, climb the slope for each year

line_filled = []
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        line_filled.append((years, on_line(years)))
    else:
        line_filled.append((years, income))

print("Height", round(height, 1), "and slope", round(slope, 2))
print("At 29 years the line says", round(on_line(29), 1))

from page import my_fill                      # where you left the star in Fig. 3
i = holes[-1]                                 # the row you filled by hand: 29 years
print("Row", i, "- you said", my_fill, " average", round(avg, 1), " line", round(on_line(29), 1), " real", truth[i])

frames = []
for step in range(7):
    t = step / 6                              # 0 at the start, 1 at the end
    stars = []
    for i in holes:
        y = avg + (line_filled[i][1] - avg) * t    # slide from the average to the line
        stars.append((points[i][0], y))
    frames.append({
        "points": complete, "stars": stars,
        "lines": [[(0, height), (32, on_line(32))]],
        "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),

```
:::
:::

The last line puts your own guess from Fig. 3 beside the two fills and the real income. Check the line by hand: the height is 30.9 and the slope 2.09, so at 29 years the line is at 30.9 + 2.09 × 29 = 91.6. That is the number in Fig. 3. The picture plays the stars sliding from the average onto the line: each person now gets an income that fits how long they have worked.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
With $\bar{x}$ for the middle of the years and $\bar{y}$ for the middle of the incomes, the line that runs closest to the complete rows has

$$\text{slope} = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y})}{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad \text{height} = \bar{y} - \text{slope} \times \bar{x}$$

and a hole at $x$ is filled with $\text{height} + \text{slope} \times x$. Read the big Σ as "add these up, over the complete rows".
:::

## What did the filling do to the data?

Look at the stars in the last two pictures. Every one sits *exactly* on the average, or *exactly* on the line. Real people never do that. The table now looks tidier than it really is.

Two numbers show how much tidier. The first is the **spread**: how far incomes typically sit from their average. Work one by hand. Two incomes, 2 and 8. The average is 5, and each is 3 away. Square the distances (3 × 3 = 9, twice), take their average (9), and undo the squaring with a square root: which number times itself makes 9? **3**. The two incomes typically sit 3 from their average.

The second is the **typical miss**: the same sum, done on how far each point sits from the closest line instead of from the average. A small typical miss means the points hug the line, so the link between years and income looks strong.

`import math` brings in Python's maths tools; `math.sqrt` is the square root. The cell compares the real incomes (from `truth`, which you would never have) with both filled tables.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
import math

def spread(values):
    m = average(values)
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total = total + (v - m) * (v - m)     # squared distance from the average
    return math.sqrt(total / len(values))     # average them, undo the squaring

def typical_miss(table):
    h, s = fit(table)                         # the closest line for this table
    total = 0
    for x, y in table:
        miss = y - (h + s * x)                # how far the point is from the line
        total = total + miss * miss
    return math.sqrt(total / len(table))

real = [(points[i][0], truth[i]) for i in range(len(points))]   # the table with no holes

print("spread of the incomes:   real", round(spread(truth), 1),
      " average-filled", round(spread([p[1] for p in filled]), 1),
      " line-filled", round(spread([p[1] for p in line_filled]), 1))
print("typical miss from line:  real", round(typical_miss(real), 1),
      " average-filled", round(typical_miss(filled), 1),
      " line-filled", round(typical_miss(line_filled), 1))

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "stars": [line_filled[i] for i in holes],
    "lines": [[(0, height), (32, on_line(32))]],
    "segments": [(line_filled[i], real[i]) for i in holes],   # from each fill to the real value
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": ["spread real " + str(round(spread(truth), 1)),
              "spread filled " + str(round(spread([p[1] for p in line_filled]), 1)),
              "miss real " + str(round(typical_miss(real), 1)),
              "miss filled " + str(round(typical_miss(line_filled), 1))],
}
```
:::

Read the two lines it prints.

- Filling with the average **shrinks the spread**, from 18.9 to 16.1. Six people now sit dead on the middle, so the incomes look more alike than they are. It also blurs the link: the flat row of stars ignores years at work, so the typical miss from the line grows.
- Filling with the line keeps the spread closer, but **the link looks stronger than it is**. The typical miss falls from 7.1 to 6.0, because six of the points now sit exactly on the line. Anything you work out from this table later will be too sure of itself.

The threads in the picture run from each star to the real income. Each one is a miss that the filled table pretends is not there.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
The stars sit too neatly on the line. How could you make the filled table look like real data again?

- **Fill with the average instead.** That shrinks the spread more, and loses the link with years at work.
- **Nudge each star up or down by a random amount.** Yes. Real points miss the line by about the typical miss, sometimes up, sometimes down. Add a random nudge of that size and the stars scatter like real points.
- **Leave the holes empty.** Then you are back to throwing rows away, with the risks from Fig. 2.
:::

### How do you put the scatter back?

`import random` brings in Python's random numbers. `random.gauss(0, size)` gives a random number around 0: up or down equally often, usually smaller than `size`, now and then bigger. `random.seed(6)` fixes the "random" numbers, so you get the same ones every time you run it. How big should the nudge be? The typical miss of the complete rows from their line, which is about 7.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
import random
random.seed(6)                                # the same "random" nudges every time

size = typical_miss(complete)                 # how far real points usually sit from the line

nudged = []
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        nudged.append((years, on_line(years) + random.gauss(0, ____)))
    else:
        nudged.append((years, income))

print("size of the nudge:", round(size, 1))
print("spread:       real", round(spread(truth), 1), " nudged", round(spread([p[1] for p in nudged]), 1))
print("typical miss: real", round(typical_miss(real), 1), " nudged", round(typical_miss(nudged), 1))

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "stars": [nudged[i] for i in holes],
    "lines": [[(0, height), (32, on_line(32))]],
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": ["nudge size " + str(round(size, 1)),
              "spread " + str(round(spread([p[1] for p in nudged]), 1)),
              "miss " + str(round(typical_miss(nudged), 1))],
}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
import random
random.seed(6)                                # the same "random" nudges every time

size = typical_miss(complete)                 # how far real points usually sit from the line

nudged = []
for years, income in points:
    if income is None:
        nudged.append((years, on_line(years) + random.gauss(0, size)))
    else:
        nudged.append((years, income))

print("size of the nudge:", round(size, 1))
print("spread:       real", round(spread(truth), 1), " nudged", round(spread([p[1] for p in nudged]), 1))
print("typical miss: real", round(typical_miss(real), 1), " nudged", round(typical_miss(nudged), 1))

picture = {
    "points": complete,
    "stars": [nudged[i] for i in holes],
    "lines": [[(0, height), (32, on_line(32))]],
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (0, 110),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "income, thousands",
    "notes": ["nudge size " + str(round(size, 1)),
              "spread " + str(round(spread([p[1] for p in nudged]), 1)),
              "miss " + str(round(typical_miss(nudged), 1))],
}
```
:::
:::

The spread and the typical miss come back to about their real values. The price looks odd at first: each single star is now probably further from that person's real income than the line was. You made every guess a little worse on purpose. What you bought is a table whose spread, and whose link between the two numbers, look like the real thing. When those matter for what you do next, that is the better deal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
Each hole at $x_i$ is filled with

$$\hat{y}_i = \underbrace{\text{height} + \text{slope} \times x_i}_{\text{the line}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{\text{the nudge}}$$

where $\varepsilon_i$ is drawn at random from a bell-shaped spread around 0 whose size is the typical miss of the complete rows from their line.
:::

## How much filling is too much?

Every star is a guess. Six guesses in 24 rows is a quarter of the incomes. Fig. 4 is a bigger made-up table, 80 rows, so you can push it further. Its two measurements are just called x and y. The buttons under it choose the way of filling, and the side column compares the real table with the filled one: the average, the spread, and the typical miss from the closest line ("line miss").

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="impute-figure" data-step="3" data-steps="1:average|2:line|3:line + nudge" data-caption="Fig. 4 · move the slider and switch how the values go missing; every number is recomputed · made-up data"}
:::

Slide *missing* from 5% towards 50% and compare the two columns, true and filled, under each way of filling. At 5% they stay close whichever way you pick. The further you go, the further they drift apart.

Then switch *at random* to *when high*. None of the three ways of filling brings the average back to the truth. Each one learns only from the rows that are left, and those are the low ones.

The cell below does the same on the 24 people. It hides more and more of the real incomes, by chance, fills them with the line, and measures the typical miss each time. `random.sample(range(24), 24)` shuffles the row numbers, `order[:m]` takes the first m of them, and `i not in gone` asks whether row i is not on that list.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
random.seed(3)
order = random.sample(range(len(real)), len(real))   # the 24 row numbers, shuffled

bars = []
frames = []
for m in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]:
    gone = order[:m]                                 # these rows lose their income
    left = [real[i] for i in range(len(real)) if i not in gone]
    h, s = fit(left)                                 # the line from what is left
    table = []
    for i in range(len(real)):
        x, y = real[i]
        if i in gone:
            table.append((x, h + s * x))             # fill with the line
        else:
            table.append((x, y))
    share = round(100 * m / len(real))               # out of every 100 incomes, how many are guesses
    print(m, "filled,", share, "in 100:  typical miss", round(typical_miss(table), 1))
    bars.append((share, typical_miss(table)))
    frames.append({
        "bars": list(bars), "hlines": [typical_miss(real)],
        "xlim": (0, 55), "ylim": (0, 9),
        "xlabel": "how many in 100 are guesses", "ylabel": "typical miss from the line",
        "notes": [str(share) + " in 100 filled", "real miss " + str(round(typical_miss(real), 1))],
    })
```
:::

The bars fall below the level line, the real typical miss, as more of the table is filled. The more you fill, the more of your "data" is your own guesswork, and the more sure of itself it looks.

A common rule of thumb: **fill in no more than about 5 in every 100 values of any one measurement.** Each filled value carries some error, and past a small slice those errors add up. Beyond that, keep the fact that the value was missing as part of the data instead (the next section), rather than hiding it behind a guess.

How do you measure the error from filling, added to the error of whatever you build on the table afterwards? There is no clean way. Test the finished result on rows it never saw, and accept that those rows probably have holes too. Remember that every table has errors already: sensors drift, people type the wrong number, two thermometers disagree. The useful question is not "is my filling perfect?" but "is it worse than the errors already in the data?" Usually it is not.

## Can a blank tell you something?

Go back to the high earners who skipped the income box. That they skipped it is itself a clue. You can keep the clue as a new measurement: a column that says, for every row, "was it missing?", 1 for yes and 0 for no.

The cell below builds that column for Fig. 2's table, where the high earners left it blank, and compares the years at work of the two groups.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import points_high                  # Fig. 2: the high earners left it blank

was_missing = []
for years, income in points_high:
    if income is None:
        was_missing.append(1)                 # 1: they left it blank
    else:
        was_missing.append(0)                 # 0: they wrote it in

blank = [points_high[i][0] for i in range(len(points_high)) if was_missing[i] == 1]
given = [points_high[i][0] for i in range(len(points_high)) if was_missing[i] == 0]

print("was it missing?", was_missing)
print("left it blank: worked", round(average(blank), 1), "years on average")
print("wrote it in:   worked", round(average(given), 1), "years on average")

picture = {
    "points": [(points_high[i][0], was_missing[i]) for i in range(len(points_high))],
    "labels": was_missing,                    # a different mark for each group
    "vlines": [average(blank), average(given)],
    "xlim": (0, 32), "ylim": (-0.5, 1.5),
    "xlabel": "years at work", "ylabel": "was it missing? 1 = yes",
    "notes": ["blank: " + str(round(average(blank), 1)) + " years",
              "given: " + str(round(average(given), 1)) + " years"],
}
```
:::

The people who left it blank had worked about twice as long. The blanks are not random noise: they carry information, and a model can use it.

For a measurement that comes in kinds, such as a colour or a town, that is easy: add "missing" as one more kind. For a number, there are three parts:

1. Put a placeholder, such as 0, in each hole, so the row can be used.
2. Add the "was it missing?" column.
3. Let every other measurement count differently when the value was missing.

The third part is what makes it work. With only the new column, a line can do no more than move up or down for the rows with a blank. The placeholder zeros then pull the other measurements' slopes in odd directions to make up for it. With the third part, the model is in effect two models: one for rows that have the value, one for rows that do not. Think of a tree with one branch.

## What you just built

Everything you did has a name:

| What you did | What it is called |
|:--|:--|
| Throwing away every row with a hole | Listwise deletion |
| Holes that fall by pure chance | Missing completely at random (MCAR) |
| Holes that depend on something else you recorded | Missing at random (MAR) |
| Holes that depend on the missing value itself | Missing not at random (MNAR) |
| Writing a value into a hole | Imputation |
| Filling with the average of the rest | Mean imputation (the median and the most common value are cousins) |
| Filling with what a line says | Regression imputation |
| Adding a random nudge the size of the typical miss | Perturbation |
| The spread | Standard deviation |
| The typical miss from the line | Residual standard error (near enough) |
| How tightly points hug the line | Correlation |
| The "was it missing?" column | A missing-value indicator |
| Letting other measurements count differently when it was missing | Interaction terms |

The names are for talking to other people and for looking things up. In R, `na.omit` throws away the rows with holes. In Python, the pandas library has `dropna` and `fillna`, and scikit-learn has a `SimpleImputer` that fills with the average, the middle value or the most common one, and can add the "was it missing?" column for you. Its `IterativeImputer` fills each column from the others, much as your line did. Whatever you use, ask first why the values are missing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reference: the same ideas in R"}
Every number and plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

A thousand made-up people whose income depends on age and years of experience. Here you have the truth.

```{r}
#| label: setup-toy-data

set.seed(2026)

n <- 1000
age     <- runif(n, 25, 65)
job_yrs <- runif(n, 0, 40)

# True income: depends on age and years of experience
income  <- 20000 + 1500 * age + 800 * job_yrs + rnorm(n, 0, 10000)

dat <- data.frame(age, job_yrs, income)
head(dat)
```

Hide some incomes three ways (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and compare the mean of what is left with the true mean.

```{r}
#| label: create-missingness

# MCAR: drop 20% of incomes completely at random
mcar  <- dat
mcar$income[sample(n, 200)] <- NA

# MAR: older people skip more often (missingness depends on age, which we observe)
p_miss_mar <- plogis(-5 + 0.1 * dat$age)
mar <- dat
mar$income[as.logical(rbinom(n, 1, p_miss_mar))] <- NA

# MNAR: high-income people skip more often (missingness depends on income itself)
p_miss_mnar <- plogis(-6 + 0.00008 * dat$income)
mnar <- dat
mnar$income[as.logical(rbinom(n, 1, p_miss_mnar))] <- NA

mean_true <- mean(dat$income)
mean_mcar <- mean(mcar$income, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_mar  <- mean(mar$income,  na.rm = TRUE)
mean_mnar <- mean(mnar$income, na.rm = TRUE)

round(c(True = mean_true, MCAR = mean_mcar, MAR = mean_mar, MNAR = mean_mnar))
```

The same four means as a bar chart, with the true mean as the dashed line.

```{r}
#| label: plot-missingness
#| fig-cap: "Listwise-deletion bias by missingness regime. MCAR is safe; MNAR is the dangerous case."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

means <- c(True = mean_true, MCAR = mean_mcar, MAR = mean_mar, MNAR = mean_mnar)
bars <- barplot(means, col = c("#2d6a4f", "#4d9978", "#e08a3c", "#d62828"),
                border = "gray30",
                main = "Mean income after listwise deletion",
                ylab = "Mean income ($)",
                ylim = c(0, max(means) * 1.15))
text(bars, means + max(means) * 0.03, labels = round(means), cex = 0.85)
abline(h = mean_true, col = "gray30", lty = 2)
```

Listwise deletion on the MNAR data: fewer rows, and a biased mean.

```{r}
#| label: listwise

# Listwise deletion is just na.omit in R
complete_cases_mnar <- na.omit(mnar)
cat("Original rows:       ", nrow(mnar), "\n")
cat("After listwise drop: ", nrow(complete_cases_mnar), "\n")
cat("Biased mean income:  ", round(mean(complete_cases_mnar$income)), "\n")
```

The indicator approach on the MAR data, first without interactions and then with them.

```{r}
#| label: indicator-approach

# Start with the MAR dataset
mar_ind <- mar
mar_ind$income_missing <- as.integer(is.na(mar_ind$income))
mar_ind$income[is.na(mar_ind$income)] <- 0

# Without interactions — income coefficient gets contaminated by the zeros
fit_bad <- lm(job_yrs ~ age + income + income_missing, data = mar_ind)

# With interactions — effectively two models
fit_good <- lm(job_yrs ~ age + income + income_missing +
                         income:income_missing + age:income_missing,
               data = mar_ind)

summary(fit_good)$coefficients |> round(4)
```

Mean imputation on the MNAR data. The mean of the filled-in column stays where the kept rows had it.

```{r}
#| label: mean-impute

mean_impute <- function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  x
}

imputed_mean <- mnar
imputed_mean$income <- mean_impute(imputed_mean$income)

cat("True mean income:        ", round(mean_true), "\n")
cat("Mean-imputed mean income:", round(mean(imputed_mean$income)), "\n")
```

Regression imputation: fit on the complete rows, predict for the rows with a missing income.

```{r}
#| label: regression-impute

# Fit a model on the complete rows
complete_rows <- mnar[!is.na(mnar$income), ]
missing_rows  <- mnar[is.na(mnar$income),  ]

impute_model <- lm(income ~ age + job_yrs, data = complete_rows)

# Predict for the missing rows
predicted_income <- predict(impute_model, newdata = missing_rows)

imputed_reg <- mnar
imputed_reg$income[is.na(imputed_reg$income)] <- predicted_income

cat("Mean of imputed incomes (regression):", round(mean(predicted_income)), "\n")
cat("Range:",
    round(min(predicted_income)), "to",
    round(max(predicted_income)), "\n")
```

Regression plus perturbation: the same predictions with noise drawn at the residual standard error.

```{r}
#| label: perturb-impute

# Residual standard error from the imputation model
res_sd <- summary(impute_model)$sigma

set.seed(2026)
perturbed <- predicted_income + rnorm(length(predicted_income), 0, res_sd)

imputed_pert <- mnar
imputed_pert$income[is.na(imputed_pert$income)] <- perturbed

cat("Regression-only SD in imputed values:      ", round(sd(predicted_income)), "\n")
cat("Regression+perturbation SD in imputed vals:", round(sd(perturbed)), "\n")
cat("Full dataset SD (true):                    ", round(sd(dat$income)), "\n")
```

The hidden incomes against what each of the three methods put in their place.

```{r}
#| label: plot-impute-compare
#| fig-cap: "Three imputation strategies compared against the true distribution. Mean imputation collapses to a spike; regression collapses to a narrow band; perturbation restores the spread."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

missing_idx <- is.na(mnar$income)
true_missing_values <- dat$income[missing_idx]

plot(density(true_missing_values, bw = 5000), lwd = 2, col = "gray30",
     main = "Distribution of the hidden incomes (and what we imputed)",
     xlab = "Income")
lines(density(rep(mean(complete_rows$income), sum(missing_idx)), bw = 5000),
      lwd = 2, col = "#d62828")
lines(density(predicted_income, bw = 5000),
      lwd = 2, col = "#e08a3c")
lines(density(perturbed, bw = 5000),
      lwd = 2, col = "#2d6a4f")
legend("topright",
       legend = c("True hidden values",
                  "Mean imputation",
                  "Regression",
                  "Regression + perturbation"),
       col = c("gray30", "#d62828", "#e08a3c", "#2d6a4f"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```
:::
